title: Alerting and on-call
subtitle: Page a human only when users are hurting and a person must act now, and build an on-call rota your team can keep up for years.

c.v: Ravi is
on call
for a payments team. His phone rings 23 times on Monday night. "CPU > 80% on db-replica-3." "Disk 85% on worker-7." "Queue length > 1,000." Each alert clears by itself a few minutes later.
By 2 a.m. Ravi mutes his phone. He has learned that these alerts never mean anything.
At 4:10 a.m., a bad config change makes 12% of card payments fail. There is no alert on failed payments, only on machines. The one CPU alert that fires looks like every other one.
The team finds out at 9 a.m. from support tickets. Ravi did nothing wrong. The alerts trained him to ignore them. (This story is made up, but the pattern is common.)
Google's SRE book names three kinds of monitoring output
. Choose one on purpose for each signal:
Page (an alert):
wakes a person up. A human must act now, because the problem is happening or about to happen
Ticket:
goes to a queue. A human must act, but no harm is done if they act within a few days
Log:
nobody needs to look. It is kept for when you debug or investigate later
Google's SRE book says your monitoring answers two questions: "what's broken, and why?"
The "what" is the
symptom
: payments fail, pages are slow. The "why" is the
cause
: a full disk, a hot CPU, a bad config.
Page on symptoms. Use causes to help you debug
, for example on dashboards. The Prometheus docs give the same advice: alert on high
latency
and errors "as high up in the stack as possible"
The book also says, "Every page should be actionable." If a page only needs a fixed, robotic response, it should not be a page
. Automate that response instead.
The key idea.
A person can react with urgency only a few times a day before they get tired
. Every useless page spends that attention. Too many useless pages cause alert fatigue, and then real pages get missed.
1. Ask four questions before you add a page
The SRE book gives a checklist. Here it is in short
Does it catch something urgent, actionable and visible to users, that nothing else catches?
Will I ever ignore it because I know it is harmless?
Can I actually do something about it?
Is someone else already paged for the same problem?
If any answer is wrong, make it a ticket, a dashboard, or delete it.
2. Page on SLO burn rate
You already know
SLOs
and
burn rate
from
Observability and SLOs
. A burn-rate alert is the best symptom alert, because it measures user pain directly.
A good alert has high precision (few false pages) and high recall (few missed problems). It should also fire fast and stop fast after the fix
. One window cannot do all four. So the SRE Workbook uses a
multiwindow
, multi-burn-rate
design. Each rule fires only when a long and a short window both pass the same burn rate
. For a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, it recommends
1 hour
5 minutes
Page
6 hours
30 minutes
Page
3 days
6 hours
Ticket
Check the first row yourself. One hour is 1/720 of 30 days. At burn rate 14.4, one hour spends 14.4 ÷ 720 = 2% of the budget. In error terms, 14.4 × 0.1% = 1.44% of requests failing.
The short window is 1/12 of the long one
. It makes the alert stop about 5 minutes after the errors stop, not an hour later
Step through a fast, a slow and a tiny burn. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
The cost is many numbers to manage

. Our advice: put them in shared recording rules, not in every team's copy. With very low traffic, one failure is a large share of requests. The Workbook suggests four fixes: synthetic traffic, combining small services for alerting, changing the product so one failure matters less, or a lower SLO or longer window
3. Group, route and silence
One broken network link can fire hundreds of alerts at once. Prometheus Alertmanager can group them by labels such as
cluster
and
alertname
, so you get one page, not hundreds
. It also has
inhibition
: if a "cluster not reachable" alert fires, it can mute every other alert for that cluster.
Silences
mute alerts for a set time, for example during planned work
The routing tree sends each alert to a receiver, such as PagerDuty for pages or email for less urgent alerts
. By default, Alertmanager waits 30 seconds to gather a new group, 5 minutes before it sends updates to that group, and 4 hours before it repeats a notification
Use a
severity
label to route. PagerDuty's own scheme has High (act now, any hour), Medium (act within 24 hours, work hours only), Low, and Notification, which never pages anyone
4. Make each alert useful at 3 a.m.
PagerDuty says alerts with generic titles cause confusion. Each alert should say what is wrong and why it matters. It should also list the steps or link to a
runbook
. Prometheus adds: link to a console that shows which part is at fault
Test every new alert. PagerDuty says, "An untested alert is equivalent to not having an alert at all"
. Also check that the alert resolves by itself when the
metric
is normal again
5. Design the rota
Google caps on-call at 25% of an SRE's time, and operations work in total at 50%

. Say two people are always on call, a primary and a secondary, in week-long shifts. Then one site needs at least eight engineers, so each one is on call one week in four. With two sites, Google suggests at least six per site
Two sites far apart can run
follow-the-sun
. Each team covers its own day, so nobody works night shifts, which harm health
Set a load limit. Google aims for at most 2 incidents per 12-hour shift. A real incident, with its cleanup and
postmortem
, takes about 6 hours
. The book's example targets for overload are fewer than 2 paging events per shift and fewer than 5 tickets a day. Noisy alerts should be tuned toward one alert per incident
Typical response times at Google are 5 minutes for user-facing services and 30 minutes for less urgent ones
. PagerDuty recommends a 5-minute
timeout
before a page goes to the backup. It says you sometimes cannot answer in time, and that is why there is a backup
. At handoff, tell the next person about issues that are still open
Pay for it. Google gives time off or cash for on-call hours, capped at a share of salary
One site, primary only
Fewer.
backup when the primary misses a page. Burnout.
One site, primary and secondary
At least 8 for 25% on-call
Night shifts still hurt sleep and health.
Two sites, follow-the-sun
, if the sites cover the clock.
At least 6 per site
Handoffs between sites lose context.
Everyone on call, no rota
Whole team.
Nobody owns the page, so everyone waits for someone else.
On-call too rare (big team, few pages)
Few.
Many.
People forget the system. Google calls this underload

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Count two numbers every week: pages per 12-hour on-call period, and pages per real incident. A week-long rota has 14 such periods. Compare them with Google's numbers: fewer than 2 pages per shift, and close to 1 alert per incident
Hold a short review after each shift. For each page ask: was it real, did it need a human, was the runbook right? Then fix, downgrade or delete the alert.
Delete alerts and dashboards nobody uses. Google says rarely used alerting is "up for removal"
Turn repeat noise into work. PagerDuty says an alert that keeps firing for a preventable non-issue, like a disk filling up, should become a fix task
. Many teams call this toil. A coming lesson on runbooks and toil covers it.
Monitor your monitoring. Prometheus suggests alerts on Alertmanager itself and an outside blackbox check
. At GitLab in 2017, backup failures were sent only by email. The emails were rejected because of an email setting (DMARC), so nobody knew the backups were failing
Give the person who was up all night the morning off.

"Here is our Alertmanager config and the last 30 days of alerts as CSV. Group the alerts by name. For each, show how often it fired, how often someone acted, and whether it is a symptom or a cause. Suggest which to delete or downgrade to a ticket."

"Write Prometheus alert rules for a 99.9% checkout SLO. Use the SRE Workbook's three multiwindow rules. Page at 14.4 over 1 h and 5 m, and at 6 over 6 h and 30 m. Open a ticket at 1 over 3 d and 6 h. Add a runbook_url and summary annotation to each."
The burn-rate thresholds match your SLO. For 99.9%, a burn rate of 14.4 is an error rate of 1.44%. For 99.5%, the same burn rate is 7.2%.
Both windows in each rule use the same burn rate.
Every page has a runbook link that really opens, and the runbook names real commands and dashboards.
group_by
labels make sense. Grouping by too little merges unrelated problems; grouping by too much sends hundreds of pages.
The agent did not add new cause alerts (CPU, disk) as pages.

q.v: Which of these should page a human at 3 a.m.?

options.v: CPU on one database replica is at 92%.
8% of checkout requests have failed for the last 10 minutes.
A nightly report job finished 20 minutes late.

why.v: Only the checkout errors are urgent, user-visible and need a human now. The other two can be a ticket or a dashboard.

q.v: Your SLO is 99.9% over 30 days. An alert fires at burn rate 14.4 over 1 hour. How much of the error budget has that hour used?

why.v: One hour is 1/720 of 30 days. 14.4 × 1/720 = 0.02, so 2% of the budget.

q.v: Why does a burn-rate page check a 5-minute window as well as a 1-hour window?

options.v: So the page stops soon after the errors stop.
So it pages for smaller error rates.
So it uses less memory in Prometheus.

why.v: The 1-hour average stays high long after a fix. The 5-minute average drops within minutes, so the alert clears fast.

q.v: Last week your on-call got 30 pages. Only 6 needed someone to act. What is the best next step?

options.v: Ask the on-call to read alerts faster.
Fix, downgrade or delete the 24 alerts that needed no action.

why.v: Google's SRE book says every page should be actionable. Noise teaches people to ignore real pages.

q.v: A team in one office wants a 24/7 rota where nobody is on call too often. What is the smallest size Google's SRE book suggests?

why.v: With on-call at most 25% of time and a primary and secondary, the book gets a minimum of eight engineers for one site.
